demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Triggers.value: Physical pain in a part of the body

Threat.value: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me

Memory.value: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.
When I remember the event I feel intense rage
When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief

Negative Appraisals.value: There is something about me that made the event happen
I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me

vignette:
David, a 54-year-old forester, had spent thirty years reading the forest—its wind patterns, the lean of trees, the hidden rot in a trunk. But one afternoon, a sudden gust twisted the crown of a towering pine he was felling, sending the trunk off its intended fall. His partner, a younger man named Eric, was standing thirty feet away, in what should have been safe ground. The butt of the tree swung sideways and caught Eric across both legs, shattering his femur and crushing his knee. David heard the crack over the chainsaw's whine, saw Eric's face go white before he even hit the ground. In the weeks that followed, David could not stop replaying that moment. When he closed his eyes, his arms would rise involuntarily, as if still gripping the saw's handles—a bodily reenactment that left him trembling with rage at himself and a grief that felt bottomless. What frightened him most was the conviction that had taken root: there was something about him that had made it happen, some intrinsic fault that had waited decades to show itself. He was no longer capable of doing the things that defined him, and he could not rely on himself to keep others safe.

The triggers were everywhere. Physical pain in his lower back—an old injury from years of carrying heavy gear—would flare when he bent to load equipment, and in that instant he would feel his body lock into the same position as when the tree had twisted. He would see a man in a blue hard hat like Eric's and the memory would crash over him, bringing the rage and the grief fresh. Physical proximity to the site of the accident, even just driving the logging road that passed near it, made his chest tighten and his eyes dart to the treetops. These reminders did more than bring the past to mind; they convinced him anew that he was fundamentally broken. Each time he drove past that stretch of forest, the thought came: You did this. You can't trust yourself. And each time, a new layer of threat settled over him. Even at home, in his own living room, he could not relax. He had begun watching people—strangers in the grocery store parking lot, coworkers at the equipment shed—for signs of danger, certain that they could see his failure written on him. A stranger approaching to ask for directions made his pulse spike; he felt threatened by ordinary encounters because, he reasoned, if something went wrong it would be his fault again. The background hum of danger he carried everywhere made ordinary cues feel like messages—a heavy footstep on gravel, a dropped tool—each one confirming what his body already believed.

The memory itself acted as a trigger. When the image of Eric's crumpled legs surfaced, his body would reenact the position—arms up, knees braced—which then sent a fresh jolt of physical pain through his back, creating a new somatic trigger that looped back into threat. The more he watched others for signs of harm, the more he noticed small lapses in safety protocols among his crew, which fed his belief that he could no longer do the job he had loved. In time, David began avoiding any situation that required him to lead a team. He took only solo inventory tasks, staying away from the felling areas. His wife noticed he had stopped laughing, stopped reaching for her at night. She found him standing at the kitchen window at 2 a.m., scanning the dark yard. When she asked what he was looking for, he could not say. What he felt was a constant readiness, a coiled alertness from which no place felt safe. On nights when the threat felt highest, the memory of Eric’s legs folding under the tree was hardest to keep at bay—it would surface in the dark, vivid and unwelcome.

What finally brought David to the clinic was a morning in the tool shed when a new hire—a young man with a blue hard hat—stepped too close to him. David had shouted, backed away, and then stood shaking under the weight of his own rage and shame. He was afraid he would hurt someone again, not physically but by being so unraveled that he made a catastrophic mistake. He desperately wanted to believe he could go back to the forest without this constant terror, but he could not imagine what that would feel like.

violations.explanation: No paragraph shows that the patient's sense of threat leads to intrusive memories of the trauma; memories are triggered by external cues, not by the threat state itself.

No paragraph shows that the patient's sense of threat creates new triggers; triggers are independently present (physical pain, blue hard hat, proximity to site) and are not described as caused by threat.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Threat → Memory: No paragraph shows that the patient's sense of threat leads to intrusive memories of the trauma; memories are triggered by external cues, not by the threat state itself.
  e.g. "Walking home on high alert, she passed a doorway and the memory was simply there — pulled out of her by the adrenaline, fully formed."
  e.g. "The persistent sense of danger kept her close to the event in her mind, as if she needed to keep reviewing it to stay one step ahead of whatever came next."
  e.g. "On nights when the threat felt highest, the memory was hardest to keep at bay — it would surface in the dark, vivid and unwelcome."
- Threat → Triggers: No paragraph shows that the patient's sense of threat creates new triggers; triggers are independently present (physical pain, blue hard hat, proximity to site) and are not described as caused by threat.
  e.g. "Already running on threat, she found that almost anything could tip into a warning — a van parked at an odd angle, a light left on that shouldn't have been."
  e.g. "The background hum of danger she carried everywhere made ordinary cues feel like messages — each one confirming what her body already believed."
  e.g. "Living at that pitch of alertness, she found the world had become dense with reminders she couldn't stop reading."
